title: Session 7: Sentence Errors and Effective Sentences
summary: How to find and fix the three big sentence errors — fragments, run-ons and comma splices — and how to choose simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences for effect, so your writing is clear, varied and academic.

blocks.title: By the end of this session you can …
items: Find and fix fragments, run-ons (fused sentences) and comma splices
Explain what each sentence structure does in a piece of writing
Vary sentence length and sentence openings
Improve a weak paragraph using all four structures

rows: **Fragment**
part of a sentence punctuated as if it were complete (no IC)
Because the bus was late. · Running to the station. · The man with the red umbrella.
**Run-on** (fused sentence)
two ICs joined with **no punctuation and no conjunction**
The bus was late we missed the lesson.
**Comma splice**
two ICs joined with **a comma only** (or comma + however)
The bus was late, we missed the lesson. · The bus was late, however we arrived on time.
a DC alone
Because the bus was late.
Join it to an IC: We missed the lesson **because** the bus was late.
no subject
Went to the shop after school.
Add a subject: **We** went to the shop after school.
no main verb
The man with the red umbrella.
Add a verb: The man with the red umbrella **waved** at us.
an -ing or to phrase alone
Running to catch the bus.
Running to catch the bus, **she dropped her phone**.
an example alone
For example, apples and bananas.
Some fruits are rich in fibre, for example, apples and bananas.

blocks.text: 3. Fixing run-ons and comma splices: five ways
The bus was late we missed the lesson. / The bus was late, we missed the lesson.

rows: 1. full stop
The bus was late**. We** missed the lesson.
2. comma + FANBOYS
The bus was late**, so** we missed the lesson.
3. semicolon
The bus was late**;** we missed the lesson.
4. semicolon + conjunctive adverb + comma
The bus was late**; as a result,** we missed the lesson.
5. make one clause dependent
**Because** the bus was late**,** we missed the lesson. / We missed the lesson **because** the bus was late.

blocks.title: Proofreading trick
items: Read your writing **backwards**, one sentence at a time. A fragment is easier to spot when it is not next to the sentence it belongs to.
Put your finger on every comma and ask: is there an IC on **both** sides? If yes, you need a FANBOYS after the comma, or change the comma to a semicolon or full stop.

rows: **Simple**
state a key point clearly; create emphasis or tension; write a strong topic or concluding sentence
Plastic is killing our oceans.
**Compound**
balance two ideas of equal importance; show addition, contrast, choice or result
Plastic is cheap, but it is extremely harmful.
**Complex**
show the exact link between ideas (cause, condition, contrast, time); add detail; sound academic
Because plastic takes centuries to break down, it builds up in the sea.
**Compound-complex**
explain a detailed argument with several linked ideas (use it sparingly)
Although governments have banned some plastic bags, millions still reach the sea, and marine animals continue to suffer.

blocks.title: Rules for effective academic writing
items: **Variety:** mix all four structures. Too many simple sentences sound childish; too many long sentences are hard to follow.
**Vary the length:** follow two long sentences with a short one for emphasis.
**Vary the openings:** don't start every sentence with I or The. Start with a DC (Although …), a conjunctive adverb (However, …), or a phrase (In many countries, …).
**One idea, one link:** never although … but or because … so.

blocks.title: Weak paragraph (first draft)
text: Mobile phones are useful. Students use them every day. They can be a problem in class. Students check social media they don't listen to the teacher. Because they want to see notifications. Phones can also be used for learning, students can search for information. Schools should not ban phones completely. They should make rules.
notes: Six simple sentences in a row → choppy and childish.
Students check social media they don't listen → run-on.
Because they want to see notifications. → fragment.
…for learning, students can search… → comma splice.

blocks.title: Improved paragraph (second draft)
text: Mobile phones are part of every student's life. **(S)** Although they are useful, they can be a serious problem in class **(CX)**. When a notification appears, many students check social media, and they stop listening to the teacher **(CC)**. On the other hand, phones can be excellent learning tools; students can search for information in seconds **(C)**. Therefore, schools should not ban phones completely **(S)**. Instead, they should create clear rules that allow phones only when teachers ask for them **(CX)**.
notes: Opens with a short, clear simple sentence → states the topic.
Although …, they can … → complex sentence shows the contrast (DC, IC, comma).
When …, many students check …, and they stop … → compound-complex explains cause and result in one sentence.
; students can search … → semicolon joins two closely related ICs.
Therefore, / On the other hand, / Instead, → conjunctive adverbs as sentence starters with commas.
rules that allow phones … → relative clause adds precise detail.
Every error from the first draft is fixed and all four structures are used.

items.q: Fragment, run-on, comma splice or correct? After the long and tiring journey home.
items.a: **fragment** → After the long and tiring journey home, we slept for ten hours.

items.q: Fragment, run-on, comma splice or correct? The shop was closed we went to another one.
items.a: **run-on** → The shop was closed, so we went to another one.

items.q: Fragment, run-on, comma splice or correct? The shop was closed, we went to another one.
items.a: **comma splice** → The shop was closed; we went to another one.

items.q: Fragment, run-on, comma splice or correct? Although the shop was closed, the café was open.
Fix in two different ways: I love football, my brother prefers tennis.
items.a: I love football, but my brother prefers tennis. · I love football, whereas my brother prefers tennis. / I love football; however, my brother prefers tennis.

items.q: Which structure would you use for a short, dramatic sentence in a story?
Combine into one complex sentence: The scientists tested the water. They found high levels of plastic.
items.a: When the scientists tested the water, they found high levels of plastic.

items.q: Rewrite with a different opening: I think that uniforms are a good idea because they save time.
items.a: e.g. Because they save time every morning, uniforms are a good idea.

blocks.title: Session 7 Practice Quiz
blocks.intro: 15 questions. Choose the best answer. You see your score and the explanations at the end.

questions.q: Because nobody knew the answer. This is …
The test was easy everyone passed. This is …
The test was easy, everyone passed. This is …
Since the test was easy, everyone passed. This is …
Walking along the beach at sunset. What is missing?
Which does NOT fix It was late we left?
c: It was late, so we left.
Because it was late, we left.

questions.q: Which fixes the comma splice correctly? She was tired, however she finished.
c: She was tired however she finished.
She was tired, however, she finished.
She was tired however, she finished.
She was tired; however, she finished.

questions.q: Which sentence structure is best for **emphasis** or a dramatic moment?
Which structure best shows **cause, condition or contrast** between two ideas?
Went to the library after school. How do you fix it?
A paragraph with ten simple sentences in a row is …
Which is a correct compound-complex sentence?
c: When the rain stopped we went out and we played football.
When the rain stopped, we went out, we played football.
When the rain stopped, we went out, and we played football.
The rain stopped, we went out and played.

questions.q: Which pair of joining words must NOT be used together?
Best fix for For example, cats and dogs.
c: Many pets are easy to care for, for example, cats and dogs.
